title: Time value of money and the price/yield seesaw

reading.h: Why a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now
reading.body:
This is the single idea that drives the entire bond half of the exam. **A dollar you receive in the future is worth less than a dollar today**, because a dollar today can be invested and grow. The more the going interest rate is, the more you give up by waiting — so a fixed future payment is worth *less* when rates are high and *more* when rates are low.

A bond is nothing but a set of fixed future payments: the coupons, plus the return of par at maturity. So the value of a bond is the **present value** of those fixed payments — and that value moves opposite to interest rates. Hold onto this: everything else in this lesson is a consequence of it.

**Future value (FV)** grows a sum forward: **FV = PV × (1 + r)ⁿ**. $1,000 invested at 6% for two years, compounded annually, becomes 1,000 × 1.06² = **$1,123.60**. **Present value (PV)** runs the same math backward — it discounts a future amount to today by dividing by (1 + r)ⁿ.

Compounding *frequency* matters: the more often interest compounds, the faster money grows, so the same nominal rate produces a higher *effective* return when compounded semiannually than annually. **Rule of 72** is the shortcut: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate. At 6%, money doubles in about 12 years; at 8%, about 9. Turned around, something that doubles in 12 years earned roughly 72 ÷ 12 = 6%.

Because a bond is a fixed stream of payments, its price and its yield move in **opposite directions**. Picture a seesaw: **price on one end, yield on the other, the fixed coupon as the pivot.** Push price up and yield drops; push price down and yield rises.

Why prices *fall when rates rise*: suppose you own an old bond paying $40 a year per $1,000 (a 4% coupon) and new bonds of equal quality now pay $60 (6%). No one will pay you full $1,000 for $40 a year when $60 is available elsewhere. Your bond's price must **drop** until the $40 it pays represents a competitive yield to the buyer — it sells at a **discount**. If instead new bonds only paid 2%, your 4% bond would be prized and sell at a **premium**. Coupon below market → discount; coupon above market → premium; coupon equal to market → par.

**Nominal (coupon) yield** is the fixed annual interest as a percent of par. It is set at issue and *never changes*: a 6% bond pays $60 a year for life, whatever the price does.

**Current yield (CY)** measures the coupon against what you actually pay today: **CY = annual interest ÷ current market price.** A 6% bond bought at a discount price of $850 has a current yield of 60 ÷ 850 = **7.06%** — higher than the 6% coupon, because you paid less than par. The same bond bought at a premium of $1,100 yields 60 ÷ 1,100 = **5.45%**. Discount raises current yield above the coupon; premium pushes it below.

reading.h: Yield to maturity (and yield to call)
reading.body:
**Yield to maturity (YTM)** is the total return if you hold to maturity, counting the coupons *and* the gain (on a discount bond) or loss (on a premium bond) realized when par is repaid. The exam approximation:

**YTM ≈ [annual interest + (par − price) ÷ years] ÷ [(par + price) ÷ 2]**.

A 5% bond priced at $850 with 10 years left: (50 + (1,000 − 850)/10) ÷ ((1,000 + 850)/2) = (50 + 15) ÷ 925 = **7.03%**. The discount ($150) is extra return spread over 10 years, so YTM lands above the current yield.

**Yield to call (YTC)** uses the same formula but substitutes the **call price** and the **years to call**. For a premium bond, a call takes the premium away sooner, so YTC comes in *below* YTM.

You rarely have to compute these on the exam — you have to **order** them. The rule follows straight from the seesaw:

- **Discount bond (price below par): Nominal < CY < YTM < YTC.** Yields rise as you look 'further out,' because you also collect the discount.
- **Premium bond (price above par): Nominal > CY > YTM > YTC.** Yields fall further out, because you also give back the premium.
- **Par bond: all four are equal.**

Classic stems: 'A 5% bond trading at 105 — which yield is *highest*?' → the nominal 5%. 'Which is *lowest*?' → yield to call. (One nuance to file away: the premium ordering assumes the call price is near par; a call priced well *above* the current price can flip YTC back to the top. The exam's plain premium questions use a call at or near par.)

reading.h: Basis points and a first look at taxable-equivalent yield
reading.body:
Yields move in **basis points**: **1 bp = 0.01%**, so 100 bp = 1%. A yield rising from 4.25% to 4.60% moved 35 basis points — shift the decimal two places.

One cross-over idea you'll reuse for municipals: to compare a tax-free yield with a taxable one, gross it up. **Taxable-equivalent yield = tax-free yield ÷ (1 − tax bracket).** A 4% municipal to an investor in the 32% bracket is worth 4% ÷ (1 − 0.32) = **5.88%** in taxable terms. Same seesaw logic, just adjusted for tax.

flashcards.front: Why is a future dollar worth less than a dollar today?
flashcards.back: A dollar today can be invested and grow; the higher the interest rate, the more you give up by waiting. A bond's value is the present value of its fixed future payments.
Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate. 6% → ~12 years; 8% → ~9 years.
Price and yield move opposite. Rates up → prices down. Coupon is the fixed pivot.
Coupon < market rate → discount; coupon > market → premium; coupon = market → par.
Annual interest ÷ par. Fixed at issue; never changes. 6% bond = $60/yr for life.
CY = annual interest ÷ current market price. 6% bond at $850 → 60/850 = 7.06%.
Nominal < CY < YTM < YTC (yields rise further out).
Nominal > CY > YTM > YTC (yields fall further out). Par bond: all equal.

quiz.stem: An investor owns a bond paying a 4% coupon. Newly issued bonds of the same quality now pay 6%. If the investor sells today, the price of the older bond will MOST likely:
options: Stay at par, because the coupon is still 4%
Rise, because older bonds are proven
Fall to a discount, so its yield becomes competitive with new 6% bonds
quiz.explanation: The bond is a fixed stream of payments; when market rates rise, that stream is worth less, so the price falls to a discount until the yield matches the 6% market. Par is only what the issuer repays at maturity, not what a buyer pays today, so the 'stay at par' choice is the trap.

quiz.stem: A 6% corporate bond is trading at $850. What is its current yield?
quiz.explanation: Current yield = annual interest ÷ market price = $60 ÷ $850 = 7.06%. 6.00% is the nominal (coupon) yield, which never changes; 5.88% divides price by interest or reflects a premium price — both distractors. Because the bond trades at a discount, current yield must exceed the coupon.

quiz.stem: A 5% bond with 10 years to maturity is trading at $850. Using the exam approximation, its yield to maturity is closest to:
quiz.explanation: YTM ≈ [50 + (1,000 − 850)/10] ÷ [(1,000 + 850)/2] = (50 + 15) ÷ 925 = 7.03%. 5.00% is the nominal yield and 5.88% is the current yield; on a discount bond YTM sits above both because you also collect the $150 discount at maturity.

quiz.stem: A 5% bond is trading at 105 and is callable in five years at par. Which of its yields is the HIGHEST?
quiz.explanation: This is a premium bond, so the ordering is Nominal > CY > YTM > YTC. The nominal 5% is highest; yield to call is lowest because a call at par removes the premium fastest. Picking yield to call inverts the premium rule.

quiz.stem: Using the Rule of 72, an investment that doubles in about 12 years earned an approximate annual rate of:
quiz.explanation: Rule of 72: rate ≈ 72 ÷ years = 72 ÷ 12 = 6%. Choosing 12% confuses the doubling period with the rate; 8% would double money in about 9 years.

quiz.stem: A discount bond's yields are ranked from LOWEST to HIGHEST as:
options: Yield to call, yield to maturity, current yield, nominal
Nominal, current yield, yield to maturity, yield to call
Current yield, nominal, yield to call, yield to maturity
quiz.explanation: For a discount bond the order is Nominal < CY < YTM < YTC — yields rise as you look further out because the discount is extra return. The reversed sequence describes a premium bond, and 'all equal' describes a par bond.

quiz.stem: A bond's yield rises from 4.25% to 4.60%. By how many basis points did the yield move?
quiz.explanation: 1 basis point = 0.01%. 4.60% − 4.25% = 0.35% = 35 basis points. Shift the decimal two places; 3.5 and 350 misplace it.
